newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu shrugs off dissent among Romanian leftists.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu shrugs off dissent among Romanian leftists.

text.p: Romania's ex-president Ion Iliescu won re-election as head of his leftist opposition party on Saturday, shrugging off calls for an overhaul of the party after a crushing election defeat by centrists last year.

Several moderates resigned in protest at the end of the two-day conference of the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) after delegates voted overwhelmingly to confirm Iliescu, an ex-communist, as party president.

The dissidents' group was led by Teodor Melescanu, a former foreign minister and party spokesman, and included two others who were previously top Iliescu aides -- his campaign manager Iosif Boda and Mircea Cosea, a former reform minister.

They had urged Iliescu to dump associates tainted by corruption scandals in order to revive the party's fortunes, which sagged after defeat in last November's parliamentary and presidential elections ended a seven-year grip on power.

"There can be no dialogue inside the PDSR," Melescanu told reproters after handing in his resignation late on Saturday. "We had called for a radical overhaul to turn the PDSR into a modern party, similar to Britain's Labour Party."
The PSDR is dominated by former communists around Iliescu, who swept to power during the 1989 revolution in which Stalinist ruler Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted and shot.

Iliescu dismissed the dissidents' calls for reforms as "elitist". He said the party had emerged stronger after its two-day conference, during which it patched up rifts with hardline nationalists, its former partners in the left-led coalition which ruled Romania until 1996.
"Romania's future is the nationalist left," Greater Romania party leader Corneliu Vadim Tudor said, drawing cheers from PDSR conference delegates.
The PDSR has 23 percent of the seats in parliament, which is dominated by centrists and where nationalists are a small minority.
Latest opinion surveys show Emil Constantinescu, who defeated Iliescu in a presidential election last November, leading in popularity ratings with 67 percent against Iliescu's 32 percent.
The surveys show continued popular support for the ruling centrist coalition despite the government's painful reforms, aimed at putting the economy on a solid market footing.
Thousands of Jiu Valley miners, Romania's most miliant, on Friday ended a 10-day strike which had posed the biggest challenge to the centrists since they won last year's election.
The government said pay concessions made to the miners were pegged on restructuring policies in the mining sector, and would not punch a hole in the country's austerity budget.
